idiom_name: EF Core TPT: ToTable per type or UseTptMappingStrategy() on the root
implementation_notes: EF Core maps this pattern directly: give each type its own table with ToTable (or call UseTptMappingStrategy() on the root) and the derived table receives a foreign key to the base table's primary key - the docs show RssBlogs(BlogId) with a constraint referencing Blogs(BlogId). The concrete type comes from the derived table that has the matching row, so no discriminator column is needed, and the provider generates the joins when a query crosses the hierarchy (context.Blogs.OfType<RssBlog>()). Hand-written SQL remains justified for hot report paths, because EF's own guidance warns that TPT is slower than TPH.
pitfalls: TPT makes every subclass query a join and EF warns it is slower than TPH; project only the columns a path needs instead of materialising whole entities.
Inherited and declared properties live in different tables, so composite foreign keys or indexes mixing both cannot be created in the database.
A derived type missing from the model is silently stored as the base type; register every subtype explicitly (EF does not scan for derived types).

variants.name: Hand-written ADO.NET mapper (SqlCommand / SqlTransaction)
variants.idiom_name: SqlCommand inserts into base + subtype tables inside one SqlTransaction
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the mapping is written by hand: one SqlCommand per path, SqlParameter for the key, and a SqlTransaction so the base row and the subtype row are written together (the base insert returns the generated key, which the subtype insert reuses). Reads either join the full path for a concrete type or fetch the base row plus the type code and dispatch in C#. This stays justified for batch jobs and legacy schemas, but the join text must be kept in one mapper class per type or it drifts from the schema.
pitfalls: Two inserts without a transaction (or without reading the generated key first) produce an orphaned base row or a foreign-key violation.
Hand-written joins must include every table in the path; a missing one materialises a base-typed object that silently lacks the subtype columns.
